definitions.text: Scalene triangle: All sides are of different length.
Isosceles triangles: Two sides are of equal length.
Equilateral triangle: All sides of equal length.
Acute angled triangle: All angles are of measure less than 90⁰.
Obtuse angled triangle: One angle is of measure greater than 90⁰.
Right angled triangle: One angle is of measure equal to 90⁰.
A triangle is a closed figure having three sides and three angles.
The sum of the measure of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the measure of the third side.
The Ambiguous Case (SSA) occurs when we are given two sides and the angle opposite one of these is less than 90°.

A perpendicular bisector is a line that intersects a line segment at right angle and dividing it into two equal parts. In other words, it intersects the line segment at its midpoint and forms right angles (90°) with it.
A median of a triangle is a line segment that joins a vertex to the midpoint of the side that is opposite to that vertex.

A point of concurrency is the single point where three or more lines, rays or line segments intersect or meet in a geometric figure. This concept is commonly used in triangles, where several important types of points of concurrency exist.
The point of concurrency of perpendicular bisector of the sides of a triangle is called circumcentre.
The point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is called centroid of the triangle.
An angle bisector of a triangle is a line or ray that divides an angle into two equal parts, creating two smaller angles that are congruent (each having half the measure of the original angle).
The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle is called incentre of the triangle.

Altitude is a ray drawn perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side of the triangle. There are three altitudes of the triangle which meet at a single point i.e. the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

A locus (plural loci) is a set of points that follow a given rule. In geometry, loci are often used to define the positions of points relative to one another or to other geometric figures. Some common types of loci along with detailed explanations will be discussed.
Equidistant: Let A be a fixed point and B be a set of points. If A is at equal distance from all points of B, then A is said to be equidistant from B.
The locus of a point whose distance is constant from a fixed point is called a circle.

The locus of a point whose distance from a fixed line is constant are parallel lines, ℓ and m e. g. the locus of a point P whose distance is 2.5 cm from a fixed line AB are parallel lines at a distance of 2.5 cm from AB.
The locus of a point whose distance from two fixed points is constant is called a perpendicular bisector.
The locus of a point whose distance is constant from two intersecting lines is called an angle bisector.
If two or more loci intersect at a point P, then P satisfies all given conditions of the loci.

fullMarks: Write the given measurements first, then name the triangle you are constructing.
For a construction, show the compass arcs or angle rays clearly; do not rely only on a finished-looking sketch.
Label every vertex, side length, angle and midpoint used in the construction.
When drawing a perpendicular bisector, show that the arcs from both endpoints intersect above and below the side, then join their intersections.
For concurrency questions, draw all three required lines or rays and mark their common point; state that they are concurrent and name the point (circumcentre, centroid, incentre or orthocentre).
For an altitude, show the right-angle mark where it meets the opposite side or its extension. Extend the side if the perpendicular falls outside the triangle.
For an ambiguous-case question, compare the given side with the perpendicular distance from the vertex to the ray, then state clearly whether zero, one or two triangles are possible.
Use centimetres for construction lengths and degrees for angles, and finish with a sentence identifying the required triangle, locus or centre.
mistakes: Using the wrong two sides or angle when constructing a triangle. Mark the given sides and included or opposite angle before drawing.
Drawing a perpendicular bisector through an endpoint instead of through the midpoint at 90°. Use equal-radius arcs from both endpoints and join the arc intersections.
Confusing a median with a perpendicular bisector. A median joins a vertex to the opposite side’s midpoint; it does not have to meet that side at 90°.
Drawing only one altitude or median when the question asks to verify concurrency. Draw all three and mark their common point.
Calling every triangle centre the same name. Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre, medians at the centroid, angle bisectors at the incentre and altitudes at the orthocentre.
In an SSA ambiguous case, assuming there is always one triangle. Draw the ray and the arc from the opposite vertex, then count their intersections.
Leaving the final construction unlabeled or not stating the result. Label points and write a concluding sentence naming the triangle, concurrency point or number of possible triangles.

written.text: Construct △ABC with the given measurements and verify that the perpendicular bisectors of the triangle are concurrent: m AB = 5 cm, m BC = 6 cm and m AC = 7 cm. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.
modelAnswer: Draw AB = 5 cm.
With centre A and radius 7 cm, draw an arc; with centre B and radius 6 cm, draw an arc intersecting it at C.
Join AC and BC to obtain △ABC.
Construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; mark their intersection O.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of AC and verify that it passes through O.
Thus, the perpendicular bisectors are concurrent at O, the circumcentre, and OA = OB = OC.
written.followUp: Construct △PQR with PQ = 4 cm, QR = 5 cm and PR = 6 cm, and verify that its perpendicular bisectors are concurrent. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.

rubric.why: The side lengths determine the required triangle.
rubric.description: Construct △ABC with the three given side lengths.
rubric.how: Draw AB = 5 cm, then locate C using arcs of radius 7 cm from A and 6 cm from B.

rubric.why: The intersection of two perpendicular bisectors locates the candidate circumcentre.
rubric.description: Construct two perpendicular bisectors and mark their intersection O.
rubric.how: Use equal-radius compass arcs to construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; label their intersection O.

rubric.why: Checking the third perpendicular bisector verifies concurrency.
rubric.description: Verify that the perpendicular bisector of AC passes through O.
rubric.how: Construct the perpendicular bisector of AC and show that it passes through O.

rubric.why: This states the verified result and identifies the point of concurrency.
rubric.description: State the result of the verification.
rubric.how: Conclude that the perpendicular bisectors meet at O, the circumcentre; OA = OB = OC.

written.text: Construct △ABC with the given measurements and verify that the perpendicular bisectors of the triangle are concurrent: m AB = 7.1 cm, m∠B = 135° and m BC = 6.5 cm. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.
modelAnswer: Draw AB = 7.1 cm.
At B, construct ∠ABX = 135° and mark C on ray BX such that BC = 6.5 cm.
Join AC to obtain △ABC.
Construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; mark their intersection O.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of AC and verify that it passes through O.
Thus, the perpendicular bisectors are concurrent at O, the circumcentre.

written.text: Construct △LMN of the following measurements and verify that the medians of the triangle are concurrent: m LM = 4.9 cm, m∠L = 51° and m∠M = 38°. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.
modelAnswer: Draw LM = 4.9 cm.
At L, construct an angle of 51° with LM; at M, construct an angle of 38° with ML on the same side of LM.
Mark the intersection of the two rays as N and join LN and MN.
Construct and mark the midpoints of LM, MN and NL.
Join each vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side to draw the three medians; mark the intersection of two as G.
Verify that the third median passes through G. Thus, the medians are concurrent at G, the centroid.
written.followUp: Construct △ABC with AB = 6 cm, ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°, and verify that its medians are concurrent. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.

rubric.why: These measurements determine △LMN.
rubric.description: Construct △LMN from the given side and angles.
rubric.how: Draw LM = 4.9 cm and construct the 51° and 38° rays at L and M on the same side of LM; their intersection is N.

rubric.why: A median must join a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
rubric.description: Mark the three side midpoints.
rubric.how: Find and mark the midpoints of LM, MN and NL.

rubric.why: The intersection of two medians gives the point to test against the third.
rubric.description: Draw the medians and mark the intersection of two as G.
rubric.how: Join each vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side, then label the intersection of two medians G.

rubric.why: The third median passing through G verifies the result and identifies the centroid.
rubric.description: State the concurrency result.
rubric.how: Show that the third median also passes through G; conclude that the medians are concurrent at G, the centroid.

written.text: Construct △LMN of the following measurements and verify that the medians of the triangle are concurrent: m MN = 4.8 cm, m∠N = 30° and m LM = 8.1 cm. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.

At N, construct a 30° ray on one side of MN.
With centre M and radius 8.1 cm, draw an arc to meet the ray at L; join LM to obtain △LMN.
Construct and mark the midpoints of LM, MN and NL.
Join each vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side to draw the three medians; mark the intersection of two as G.
Verify that the third median passes through G. Thus, the medians are concurrent at G, the centroid.

written.text: Verify that the angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent with the following measurement: m AB = 4.5 cm, m∠A = 45° and m AC = 5.3 cm. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.
modelAnswer: Draw AB = 4.5 cm.
At A, construct ∠BAX = 45° and mark C on ray AX such that AC = 5.3 cm; join BC.
Construct the bisectors of ∠A and ∠B and mark their intersection I.
Construct the bisector of ∠C and verify that it passes through I.
Thus, the angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent at I, the incentre.

written.text: Verify that the angle bisectors of △ABC are concurrent with the following measurement: m AB = 6 cm, m∠A = 150° and m∠B = 60°.
modelAnswer: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°, but 210° > 180°.
Therefore, △ABC cannot be constructed and its angle bisectors cannot be verified.

written.text: Given the measurements of △DEF : m DE = 4.8 cm, m EF = 4 cm and m∠E = 45°, draw altitudes of △DEF and find orthocentre. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.
modelAnswer: Draw EF = 4 cm.
At E, construct an angle of 45° with EF; mark D on its ray so DE = 4.8 cm, then join DF.
Through D, draw a perpendicular to EF; through F, draw a perpendicular to DE.
Mark the intersection of these altitudes H.
Through E, draw a perpendicular to DF and verify that it passes through H.
Thus, H is the orthocentre of △DEF.

written.text: Construct the following triangles and find whether there exists any ambiguous case: △BCD ; m BC = 5 cm, m∠B = 62° and m CD = 4.7 cm. Draw it on paper and photograph your work, or type your table of values / measurements.
modelAnswer: Draw BC = 5 cm and construct a 62° ray at B.
With centre C and radius 4.7 cm, draw an arc that meets the ray at two points, D₁ and D₂.
Join CD₁ and CD₂ to obtain two triangles, △BCD₁ and △BCD₂.
Both triangles satisfy the given measurements. Therefore, there are two possible triangles and the case is ambiguous.

rubric.why: This is the requested conclusion from the two valid constructions.
rubric.description: State whether the case is ambiguous.
rubric.how: Conclude that there are two possible triangles, so this is an ambiguous case.
